transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-04
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Aisha Malik (Head of ML, FinServe), Tom Baker (Platform Lead), Jorge Rivera (Security)

Auto-generated summary: Discussed POC scope, benchmarks, deployment modes and security requirements.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Maya from Redwood. Ethan and I are on the call to scope the POC and walk through hosted vs dedicated vs private options. Aisha, do you want to kick off with a quick context of what you guys are trying to achieve?

[00:18] Aisha: Sure, yeah. Hi, everyone. We're FinServe, we run a fraud-detection assistant that surfaces possible fraud flags to ops. Currently everything's on-prem with model inference in our private cluster, but we're evaluating options to move some traffic to a managed service. Main drivers are reducing infra ops, improving tail latency for customer-facing flows, and lowering per-token costs for high-volume batch jobs.

[00:40] Ethan: Got it. When you say "lower per-token cost for batch", can you quantify current RPS and batch sizes? Also any SLOs we should know about?

[00:48] Tom: For real-time flows it's around 60 RPS at peak, spiky bursts up to 250 for a few minutes. Batch is larger — we run daily re-runs of scoring, about 200k sequence items; sequence length distribution is mostly short, median 40 tokens, 95th ~380 tokens. P95 latency target for real-time is sub-300ms, p99 ideally <800ms, cost target is roughly 30% below our current self-hosted spend.

[01:15] Maya: Good, that's helpful. Quick framing: Hosted is fastest to test — you use Redwood's shared infra and API, we can run benchmarks quickly. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and predictable throughput with isolation; Private is VPC/on-prem with customer-controlled network and keys — takes more setup but required for strict compliance.

[01:41] Jorge: From security side, we need SOC2 + ISO, KMS/HSM integration, full audit logs, and VPC connectivity for Private. For Dedicated we'd need a private peering option and customer-managed keys. Also data residency: certain PII data must not leave EMEA.

[01:58] Ethan: Understood. For POC we typically run three pillars of benchmarks: functional correctness/quality (eval against your test prompts), latency/throughput under representative traffic, and cost/efficiency (token costs with batching/quantization). We'll also validate fallback and canary rollouts if you want.

[02:20] Aisha: That sounds sensible. For quality we want to make sure the model doesn't regress — we'll give you a representative eval set of about 500 prompts with our scoring rubric. For latency we need p95 under 300ms for the real-time subset.

[02:35] Tom: One question: if we start on Hosted for speed, will migrating to Dedicated/Private change model behavior or response times substantially?

[02:42] Maya: Migration path is designed to be smooth. Same API and model variants. Differences come from hardware and network topology — Dedicated will give you more predictable p99 and throughput, Private gives you control over egress and KMS. We do have verified performance profiles per model; we can share the benchmark matrix.

[03:05] Jorge: Network egress and data residency: with Hosted, data would leave our VPC. Not acceptable for some datasets. So Hosted is only an option for anonymized/eu-exempt traffic. Private or Dedicated with VPC peering would be preferred for production.

[03:22] Ethan: Makes sense. Operationally for the POC we can do a staged plan: 1) Hosted quick bench on a small subset to validate quality and baseline latency, 2) Dedicated pilot for throughput and p99 validation with peering, 3) if required, Private deploy for full compliance. Each stage has different setup times. Hosted bench can be done in days; Dedicated pilot typically 1-2 weeks to provision and test; Private (VPC/on-prem) is multi-week due to network and cert setup.

[03:50] Aisha: Timeline-wise, what's realistic? We're hoping to have something in 3-4 weeks to present to execs.

[03:56] Maya: For a minimal POC focusing on quality + latency baseline using Hosted, we can deliver results in about 1 week once we have the eval set and access. For the Dedicated pilot with peering and KMS, budget 2-3 weeks. Private will probably push beyond 4 weeks depending on your infra team's bandwidth. So 3-4 weeks for a combined plan is tight but doable if you accept staged approach.

[04:20] Tom: On cost modelling, how granular can you get? We need token-level cost breakdown and a projection for full production traffic with autoscaling.

[04:28] Ethan: We can provide token-level estimates, plus simulated monthly cost projections for your traffic profile. Important controls that affect cost: batching configuration, KV cache hit rates (we may read it as K-V but sometimes annotated differently), quantization profiles and model selection. We'll run your traces through our cost model during the POC.

[04:48] Aisha: About KV cache — we have a lot of repeated prefixes in session flows; caching could drastically change cost. Will that be part of the benchmark?

[04:56] Ethan: Yes, we'll test with cache enabled and disabled and show delta on per-token compute. Also assess batching at different concurrency levels.

[05:08] Jorge: On encryption: we need to confirm CMEK support and that logs containing tokens are redacted or never persist in cleartext. Also audit trails for who ran what.

[05:18] Maya: We'll share SOC2 artifacts and the KMS integration guide. For Hosted we have options for encrypted in-transit and at-rest, but CMEK and granular audit logs are typically available on Dedicated or Private — we'll clarify exact controls in the doc we send.

[05:33] Tom: For the baseline bench on Hosted, do you require us to open any whitelist IPs or provide API keys?

[05:40] Ethan: We'll need API keys and sample traffic traces. Optionally, we can do a whitebox run where we provision a short-lived environment or use a secure upload for traces. No peering is required for Hosted. For Dedicated we'll need peering details and for Private your infra team will need to coordinate on network and certs.

[06:02] Aisha: Success criteria — let's align. For us: (1) quality parity (no more than 5% regression on our eval rubric), (2) real-time p95 <300ms, p99 <800ms under representative traffic, (3) cost projection <=30% of current infra for production profile, (4) security controls — SOC2 and KMS or acceptable VPC isolation.

[06:26] Maya: That's a clear set. We'll codify those as the POC success criteria. For quality, we'll run automated evals and manual spot checks. For latency we'll run a 1k-request plan for a couple of load shapes including bursty traffic to capture p95/p99.

[06:44] Tom: For the load shapes, we can provide a day-of-week and hourly distribution; also which endpoints are sensitive. Expect some cold-start variance if KV warmup is required.

[06:55] Ethan: We'll capture cold start behavior and steady-state. Also recommend doing a KV priming run to show best-case and cold-start worst-case. We'll include canary rollout behavior in the Dedicated pilot to show fallback to smaller models if load spikes.

[07:12] Aisha: Any gotchas between Dedicated and Private for our use case?

[07:17] Maya: Dedicated gives you reserved capacity and single-tenant GPU pools but still managed by Redwood control plane — easier to stand up. Private pushes the control plane into your VPC or on-prem — more work but gives you full network control, egress guarantees, and strict KMS management. If data residency is the blocker, Private is the path; if you mainly need isolation and keys, Dedicated with peering + BYOK might suffice.

[07:40] Jorge: For Dedicated, does the control plane see request payloads or are they proxied through our peering? We need to ensure minimal surface area.

[07:47] Ethan: In Dedicated with private peering, we can arrange for control plane to manage metadata while payloads go directly to dedicated inference nodes; we can provide a diagram. For Private the control plane can be run in your VPC and logs stay under your retention. We'll include a security architecture diagram in the send.

[08:05] Tom: On measurable deliverables for the POC, can we agree on a written report with: 1) bench results (latency/throughput/cost), 2) quality evals with sample passes/fails, 3) architecture notes and recommended config (batching, quant, cache), 4) next steps for production?

[08:18] Maya: Absolutely. We'll produce a POC report and a recommended deployment plan.

[08:25] Aisha: One more question — do you support private model versions or model pinning to freeze behavior during rollout? We need determinism for auditability.

[08:33] Ethan: Yes, you can pin model versions and rollouts. We also support immutable model artifacts and eval history so you can correlate regression. We'll surface that in the report.

[08:44] Maya: Great. To recap next steps: Maya will send pricing + SOC2/KMS doc; Ethan will schedule the Hosted quick bench and then Dedicated pilot once peering info is available; Tom will share traces and eval set. We'll aim to kick the Hosted bench within 3 business days and aim for Dedicated pilot in week of Nov 16.

[09:05] Tom: Sounds good. I'll get the traces and a masked dataset by Monday.

[09:12] Jorge: I'll review the SOC2 and confirm any additional compliance asks.

[09:18] Maya: Perfect — we'll follow up with a calendar invite for the bench kickoff and include the POC scope doc. Any final Qs?

[09:25] Aisha: None from me. Thanks, everyone.

[09:28] Maya: Thanks all. End call.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings ("K V cache" vs "KV cache"), speaker labels approximate, natural disfluencies left in place.
